[Package Info](package-info.html) ::: EdgeCase is a graph analysis library for Python that pairs a fast Rust core with a friendly, chainable API. Build a network, run any of more than 700 methods on it, query it with Cypher, and get the answers back as Polars DataFrames and publication-ready pictures. ```{=html} ``` ::: {.ec-cta} [Get started](user-guide/quick-start.qmd){.ec-btn .ec-btn-primary} [Read the User Guide](user-guide/get-started.qmd){.ec-btn} [Browse the reference](reference/index.qmd){.ec-btn} ```{=html} ``` ::: ```{=html}

``` ### An analysis, one step at a time {.ec-heading} An analysis is a chain of methods on a graph, each storing its answer as a node or edge attribute for the next to use. Step through this one, on the karate club network that Wayne Zachary studied in the 1970s, to see what each step adds; the new lines of code are highlighted. ::::: {.ec-stepper} :::: {.ec-step} [Load]{.ec-step-name} Start with a graph: here, one of the bundled datasets, the 34 members of a karate club and who spent time with whom outside it. ::: {#848a1091 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = ( ec.karate_club() ) karate.plot( label_by="label", seed=9, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: :::: :::: {.ec-step} [Communities]{.ec-step-name} Find the club's communities with the Louvain method, and color the members by the one they're in. ::: {#5cf3f430 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = ( ec.karate_club() .cmty_louvain() ) karate.plot( color_by="cmty_louvain", label_by="label", seed=9, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: :::: :::: {.ec-step} [Centrality]{.ec-step-name} Rank the members by PageRank and size them by it: the club's instructor (0) and its administrator (33), at the centers of the two factions the club later split into, stand out. ::: {#ae61f043 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = ( ec.karate_club() .cmty_louvain() .pagerank() ) karate.plot( color_by="cmty_louvain", size_by="pagerank", label_by="label", seed=9, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: :::: :::: {.ec-step} [Tabulate]{.ec-step-name} Every answer is a column in the graph's node table, a Polars DataFrame, ready to sort, filter, join, and export. ::: {#ed1f6ef8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = ( ec.karate_club() .cmty_louvain() .pagerank() ) ( karate.get_node_df() .select("label", "role", "faction", "cmty_louvain", "pagerank") .sort("pagerank", descending=True) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: :::: ::::: [Quick start →](user-guide/quick-start.qmd){.ec-more} [Node and edge data →](user-guide/node-and-edge-data.qmd){.ec-more} ### Ask the graph with Cypher {.ec-heading} Many questions about a network are questions about a shape: a ring of payments, everyone two steps away, the shortest way through. [`match()`](reference/Graph.match.qmd) answers them with Cypher, the pattern language of Neo4j, and returns what it finds as a DataFrame. Pick a query to see its result, and what it matched in this small network of payments. :::::: {.ec-tour} ::: {.ec-stage} ::: {#0c9804a1 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="How `payments` is made"} edges = [ ("Dee", "Eve", 80), ("Eve", "Dee", 25), ("Ana", "Dee", 120), ("Dee", "Ben", 60), ("Ben", "Eve", 300), ("Gus", "Dee", 45), ("Eve", "Finn", 2000), ("Ana", "Ben", 9500), ("Ben", "Cruz", 9400), ("Cruz", "Ana", 9300), ("Finn", "Gus", 4950), ("Gus", "Hal", 4900), ("Hal", "Finn", 4850), ] # Each tuple is a payment: who paid, who was paid, and how much (the edge's weight) payments = ec.Graph.from_edges(edges, directed=True) payments.plot(label_by="label", seed=38, width=600, height=360) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: {.ec-queries} :::: {.ec-step} [Rings]{.ec-step-name} Money that goes around a circle of three accounts in large payments, and comes back to where it started. ::: {#9cf199e7 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} payments.match(""" MATCH (a)-[x]->(b)-[y]->(c)-[z]->(a) WHERE x.weight >= 1000 AND y.weight >= 1000 AND z.weight >= 1000 AND a.name < b.name AND a.name < c.name RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b, c.name AS c """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

[Cypher queries →](user-guide/cypher.qmd){.ec-more} [Selections →](user-guide/selections.qmd){.ec-more} ### Every step, recorded {.ec-heading} A graph keeps a log of the steps taken on it, so an analysis documents itself, and `play()` turns the log into an animation. This one searches outward from Ana, finds the rings of large payments, and flags the accounts in them. It plays when it comes into view; pause it, or step through it. ::: {.ec-player} ::: {#59559289 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} flagged = ( ec.Graph.from_edges(edges, directed=True) .bfs("Ana") .select_match(""" MATCH (a)-[x]->(b)-[y]->(c)-[z]->(a) WHERE x.weight >= 1000 AND y.weight >= 1000 AND z.weight >= 1000 """) .set_node_attrs_ws(flag="ring") .clear_selection() ) flagged.play(seed=38) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Speed doesn't come at the cost of correctness: more than 9,200 tests cover the library, many of them checking results against NetworkX on the same graphs, and property-based tests generate random graphs and Cypher queries to check what must always hold. ### Everything a graph needs {.ec-heading} :::: {.ec-cards} ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Graphs of every kind]{.ec-card-title} Directed or undirected, weighted or not, with parallel edges and self-loops, and attributes of any type on every node and edge. [The graph model →](user-guide/graph-model.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Algorithms]{.ec-card-title} Paths, centrality, communities, connectivity and flows, matching, coloring, spectral methods and more, each storing its answer on the graph. [Paths and distances →](user-guide/paths.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Cypher and selections]{.ec-card-title} Find patterns with Cypher, and select nodes and edges to set, delete, traverse or take as a subgraph. [Cypher queries →](user-guide/cypher.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Plots and layouts]{.ec-card-title} Self-contained SVG plots in light and dark themes, with more than a dozen layouts and full control over the aesthetics. [Static plots →](user-guide/plotting.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Interactive views]{.ec-card-title} Drag, zoom and click through a graph, with a GPU renderer for networks of hundreds of thousands of nodes. [Interactive widgets →](user-guide/interactive.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Domain toolkits]{.ec-card-title} Network biology, spreading and resilience, and multiplex networks, in the vocabulary of each field. [Network biology →](user-guide/network-biology.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Files and other libraries]{.ec-card-title} 28 readers and 28 writers, from GraphML to DOT, and conversion to and from NetworkX, igraph, NumPy, SciPy and pandas. [File formats →](user-guide/file-formats.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Generators and datasets]{.ec-card-title} 85 generators, from classic graphs to random models, and 20 real networks, ready to load. [Datasets →](user-guide/datasets.qmd) ::: ::: {.ec-card} []{.ec-card-icon} [Summary tables]{.ec-card-title} Network summaries and centrality rankings as Great Tables, ready for a report. [Summary tables →](user-guide/tables.qmd) ::: :::: ### Get started {.ec-heading} ::: {.ec-start} Install EdgeCase from PyPI: ```bash pip install edgecase ``` Then take the [quick start](user-guide/quick-start.qmd), a short tour that builds a graph, analyzes a real social network, draws it, and queries it in only a few lines each, or read the [User Guide](user-guide/get-started.qmd) from the beginning. :::
